name: materials
description: The shared PBR material system. Every opaque surface in the game is one row here, rendered by shaders/surface_base.gdshader or shaders/foliage_base.gdshader; water is shaders/water_base.gdshader, which is not a material row because it reads the hydrology mask rather than a texture set. A material is a parameter set, never its own shader, so the Mobile renderer compiles one variant per shader rather than one per material.

texture_sets.note: A texture set is three maps in the glTF convention, so a Poly Haven download maps straight on with no conversion: albedo is sRGB, normal is tangent-space, and ORM packs ambient occlusion in R, roughness in G, metallic in B.
texture_sets.why_a_ladder: 2048 for surfaces the player stands on and looks at closely; 1024 for the same material at distance; 512 for anything only ever seen as a scatter card. The tier's budget decides which rung, not the artist.
texture_sets.alpha_note: Leaf, fern and grass cards carry cut-out alpha, and mipmaps are where that goes wrong quietly: a plain box filter averages transparent texels into the leaves at each level, so a crown thins with distance and eventually dissolves. Two consequences, neither of which the shader can fix. First, mipmaps must be generated on import (Godot's default) and the alpha must be dilated before they are, or the thinning starts at the second mip. Second, until a coverage-preserving mip chain is authored, alpha_cutoff is what holds a distant card together — raising it keeps leaves at range, lowering it thins them. The real fix is a dilated mask plus a per-LOD cutoff, which is Phase 3 work when the cards exist. Recorded here because it is a texture-import decision, not a shader one, and the complaint would otherwise arrive as 'the trees vanish at 200 m'.

tiling_policy.unit: metres per tile, so a 1 m boulder and a 40 m cliff use the same texture at the same apparent detail
tiling_policy.clamp: 0.25 m to 8 m. Below 0.25 the texture visibly repeats at arm's length; above 8 it reads as noise.
tiling_policy.uv_note: the shader takes a finished uv_scale, so the importer converts tiling_m using the mesh's UV area. The shader never has to know how big the object is.

materials.name: mat_wood_bark
materials.note: bark soaks and darkens hard, unlike the sawn wood this surface also covers: the surface id is what footsteps and impact VFX key off, and a wet log's is not a wet plank's

materials.name: mat_foliage_leaf_broadleaf
materials.note: leaves bead rather than soak. The surface id is shared with the forest floor so a footstep still rustles, but a wet leaf card darkens little and gains a sheen — which is what the foliage shader's 0.55 darken scale already assumed.

materials.name: mat_foliage_leaf_conifer
materials.note: needles barely flutter; a conifer that shimmers like a broadleaf reads as plastic. Waxy needles also bead rather than soak, so they take the same wetness override as the broadleaf.

materials.name: mat_foliage_fern
materials.note: a fern is low, so its whole sway is smaller than a tree's branch sway. Its fronds bead like other leaves rather than soaking like the grass surface it shares.

materials.name: mat_foliage_grass_card
materials.note: a grass card is a leaf, not turf: it beads, while the grass surface it shares soaks. The surface id still gives the footstep its rustle.

materials.name: mat_foliage_ivy
materials.note: ivy leaves are waxy and bead like the other foliage cards, rather than soaking like the ground surface they hang over.

rules: A material is a row, not a shader. Adding a shader needs a reason that cannot be a uniform.
Every material names a surface_id from assets/surface_ids.json, so footsteps and VFX work on it without a second lookup.
tiling_m is in metres and must sit inside the clamp; tools/validate/check_materials.py enforces it.
A material used by foliage names the foliage shader; everything else names surface.
wetness_darken is per material and is the only place the value lives.
